report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Alterations in cortical brain development from ages 11 to 15 years in adolescents at familial high risk for schizophrenia or bipolar disorder
table.research_questions:
For four whole-brain measures (brain volume, cortical volume, cortical thickness, and surface area);

a.	Group by sex interactions will mirror those observed in VIA 11, suggesting sex-specific vulnerability in FHR children. In VIA 11, cross-sectionally, children at FHR-SZ and FHR-BP demonstrated sex-specific deviations in cortical structure from population-based controls (PBCs). The main results indicated smaller brain volume, cortical volume, and surface area in FHR-SZ males, and larger brain volume and cortical volume in FHR-BP females relative to PBCs. There were no group or group-by-sex differences in cortical thickness.

b.	Group by age interactions will reveal atypical slopes in FHR, characterized by greater reductions across time on each cortical structural brain measure, particularly for the FHR-SZ group relative to PBCs. While there were no group differences in cortical thickness in VIA 11, we now expect to see group differences in slope with the inclusion of data from VIA 11 and VIA 15.

c.	Results will survive the inclusion of lifetime axis-I disorders as a covariate but will become less pronounced. More pronounced effects will be seen in children at FHR with a lifetime axis-I disorder compared to without. 

d.	More pronounced effects will be seen in children at FHR with psychotic-like experiences compared to without.

More detailed hypotheses are described in the Analysis Plan

table.q5: Researchers were blinded wherever possible to participant familial high risk status for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder during data collection. Researchers were also blinded to familial high risk status during inspection of data, quality control of data, and selection of a final dataset for analysis.
table.study_design_overview: Longitudinal, register-based cohort study. Our analysis will include a group variable with three levels (FHR-SZ, FHR-BP, and population-based controls [PBC]) and two data collection time-points (when participants are aged ~11 years and ~15 years). We are interested in group differences in the change of cortical structural measures across time (within-subject), as well as interactions with sex (two levels: female and male); mixed design

table.existing_data_explanation:
We are registering prior to data analysis. As of the date of submission, the data exist and have been accessed, though no analysis has been conducted related to the research plan. We are using a larger existing dataset, which has been used for different studies over time.

We are unaware of any patterns or summary statistics in the outcome variables of interest (brain volume, cortical volume, cortical thickness, and surface area), and we have not run any of the planned analyses. To determine the final sample for our analysis we identified subjects who were outliers on the outcome variables of interest, and excluded outlier subjects if their data quality was also poor. We were blinded to subjects’ FHR status during this process. We have also looked at the descriptive and clinical characteristics of the final sample by FHR status. Beyond calculating these characteristics and identifying outlier subjects, however, we have not run any of the statistical models, and these prior observations of the final sample have not had any impact on planning the statistical models or determining our hypotheses, which are based on already published or submitted results.
table.data_collection_procedures:
The planned analysis includes children enrolled in the Danish High-Risk and Resilience study (VIA), a longitudinal, register-based cohort study which is ongoing and follows a total of 522 7-year-old children born to at least one parent with SZ (FHR-SZ, n=202), BP (FHR-BP, n=120), or neither of these disorders (PBC, n=200). Data for the first (VIA 11; 465 children, aged 11-13) and second (VIA 15; 427 children, aged 14-17) follow-ups were collected starting March 1st, 2017 and May 1st, 2021, respectively. MRI data collection occurred at two research sites: the Danish Research Centre for Magnetic Resonance (DRMCR) and the Center of Functionally Integrative Neuroscience (CFIN). The protocol papers for VIA 11 (Thorup et al., 2018) and VIA 15 (Thorup et al., 2022) have all of the information regarding data collection procedures. Written and informed consent from the children’s legal guardian(s) and oral assent from the children was obtained prior to their participation.

table.sample_size:
MRI data for 288 children in VIA 11 (FHR-SZ: n=104; FHR-BP: n=68; PBC: n=116) and for 249 children in VIA 15 (FHR-SZ: n=93; FHR-BP: n=61; PBC: n=95) will be included in the planned analysis. This final sample for the planned analysis was selected following quality control procedures. Quality control and exclusion procedures included:

a.	Initial visual inspection: Raw T1-weighted images were visually inspected by trained raters blinded to group and sex. Scans with excessive motion or poor quality were excluded, resulting in the removal of 19 scans from VIA 11 and 30 from VIA 15.

b.	Segmentation quality check: FreeSurfer cortical segmentations were assessed by raters blinded to the group or sex, using an in-house graphical user interface (GUI), which projected segmentations onto native-space T1 images. ROIs with clearly mislabeled or poorly fitting segmentations were excluded. 

c.	Statistical outlier detection (cross-referenced with segmentation quality): Standardized residuals for ROI volumes (controlling for age, sex, and MRI site) were computed to identify outliers (> ±2 SD). These cases were cross-referenced with segmentation quality from Step 2. Volumes deemed biological outliers (e.g. due to large individual differences in brain size) were retained. Non-biological outliers, likely due to segmentation errors, were excluded after visual inspection. In total, 17 scans from VIA 11 and 11 from VIA 15 were excluded with poor segmentation.

d.	Euler number screening: We computed standardised residuals of the Total Euler Number (TEN), controlling for age, sex, and site. Images with TEN residuals beyond ±3 SD and evidence of poor surface reconstruction were excluded, resulting in one exclusion from VIA 11 and one from VIA 15.
table.measured_variables:
a.	Brain measures: MRI data from VIA11 and VIA15 were preprocessed with the FreeSurfer longitudinal stream (version 7.4.1). The main outcome measures will be whole-brain (averaged across hemispheres) brain volume, cortical volume, cortical thickness, and surface area. In addition to the whole-brain measures, we are planning exploratory parcel-wise analyses with 68 total parcels (34 per hemisphere). Total intracranial volume will be extracted as well to be used as a covariate of no interest. 

b.	Group: Familial high-risk group (FHR-SZ, FHR-BP, PBC)

c.	Age: Mean-centered age at MRI in years. Transformation will be: participant_age = age in years - mean sample age.

d.	Sex: Sex assigned at birth (male and female)

e.	Site: MRI site where data was collected (DRCMR or CFIN)

f.	Euler number: The Total Euler Number (TEN) was extracted from FreeSurfer for each participant to be used as a proxy for motion during image acquisition. TEN represents the number of omission “holes” in the segmentation of the cortex, which is correlated with inaccuracies in the segmentation.

g.	Lifetime axis-I disorder: Cumulative lifetime axis-I disorder (excluding elimination disorders, unspecified tic disorder, and specific phobias) after the structured interview Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (K-SADS) was administered by a trained psychiatrist at VIA 15.

h.	Psychotic like experiences (PLE): Interview inspired by the Scale for Prodromal Symptoms.
table.indices: As mentioned above, we will take left and right hemisphere measures of cortical structure (e.g., cortical thickness) and average them to derive one overall whole-brain measure, e.g., cortical_thickness_via11=(lh_cortical_thickness_via11+rh_cortical_thickness_via11)/2
table.statistical_tests:
Step 1: Testing group by age and group by sex interactions for cortical structural measures
We plan to run linear mixed-effects models including group, sex, age, group by sex, group by age, age by sex, site, and Euler number, with random intercepts for subject nested in families in order to account for sibling pairs. There are four structural brain measures of interest, as in the VIA 11 cortical paper, which are brain volume, cortical volume, surface area, and cortical thickness. As we have four brain measures of interest, we will use FDR correction for these four measures. Using the lme4 package in R, the models will look like this: 

lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age + group*sex + age*sex + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))

We are primarily interested in interpreting the interaction terms for group by age and group by sex. We are including the group by sex interaction already in step 1 because we expect there to be sex-specific group differences given the findings from VIA 11. For group by age, we expect to see a reduction across time for each cortical structural brain measure in each group, which will be more pronounced in FHR-SZ. To ease interpretation, we will mean center age such that the main effect of group can be interpreted as the effect at the mean age, across the investigated age range. For group by sex, we expect to replicate results from VIA 11, namely to see reduced brain volume, cortical volume, and surface area in FHR-SZ males, and increased brain volume and cortical volume in FHR-BP females. We additionally expect to see reduced cortical thickness in FHR-SZ males, which was not previously seen in VIA 11 but is predicted now that data also extends to VIA 15, given the accelerated cortical thinning observed in adolescence. Age by sex is included as a control variable since we expect slopes to differ by sex (i.e., earlier maturation in females) although we are not primarily interested in this variability. We further control for MRI site and euler number.

Step 2: Testing group by age interactions, stratifying by sex 
Whether or not the group by age or group by sex interactions are significant in step 1, we will proceed to step 2, since there is a strong justification to test for sex-specific group differences in slope between VIA 11 and VIA 15 given the sex-specific effects already identified in VIA 11. To test for sex-specific group differences, we will stratify the sample by sex and run linear mixed-effects models similar to those in step 1, including group, age, group by age, site, and Euler number, with random intercepts for subject nested in families. The models will look like this:

For females only: lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))

For males only: lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))

	We expect group effects similar to those observed in VIA 11. For group by age, similar to step 1, we expect to see a reduction across time for each cortical structural brain measure in each group, which will be more pronounced in FHR-SZ, for both females and males. Since accelerated cortical thinning starts earlier for females, we predict that reduced cortical thickness will extend to FHR-SZ females as well as males. One exception to the pattern of reduced cortical structural brain measures is FHR-BP females, who we predict will not show more pronounced significant age-related reductions in brain volume or cortical volume compared to PBC females at the whole group level. This is because they had larger brain volume and cortical volume in VIA 11, and studies of adult relatives of individuals with BP have larger volumes, so FHR-BP females may be on a different maturational trajectory.      

Step 3: Testing group by age by sex interactions
Since sex differences cannot be formally tested in stratified models, we will test them in a three-way interaction (group by age by sex) in models that look like this:

lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age*sex + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id)) 

In this model, we can directly test the effect of sex-specific group differences on slope between VIA 11 and VIA 15. As noted above, we predict that FHR-SZ females will have a steeper decline than FHR-SZ males, which will also be true though to a lesser extent for females in general. This is because FHR-SZ females do not show reductions in brain volume, cortical volume, surface area, or cortical thickness already in VIA 11, while FHR-SZ males do, and because we know that females in general show an earlier inflection point of cortical thinning during adolescence, or the age at which the rate of thinning is fastest. Conversely, we predict that FHR-BP females will decline less than FHR-BP males, particularly in brain volume and cortical volume, as these measures were increased in FHR-BP females in VIA 11. Generally, however, we do not expect major sex-specific group differences in slope.

Step 4: Planned follow-up analyses
Additionally, planned follow-up up analyses will be performed based on the findings from the previous steps. For example, if we see a significant group effect in step 1, then we would take the step 1 model and adjust it according to the planned follow-up analysis (e.g., adding an additional covariate). If we see a significant group effect in step 2, then we would also add to the model from step 2. We think that models from step 2 are the most likely to yield significant results and advance to the planned follow-up analyses.

A.	Including lifetime axis-I diagnoses: 

i.	Do results survive when controlling for lifetime axis-I diagnoses? We will incorporate an additional covariate, lifetime axis-I diagnosis (excluding elimination disorders, unspecified tic disorder, and specific phobias), into new models based on those in the previous steps where there is a significant effect of group. We predict that including lifetime axis-I diagnoses will weaken the group effect, but that the group effect will remain significant. If we see significant group effects in step 1, the model controlling for axis-I would look like this:

lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age + group*sex + age*sex + axis-I + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))

If we see significant group effects in step 2 for females, the model controlling for axis-I would look like this:

For females only: lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age + axis-I + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))

ii.	Do developmental slopes differ based on axis-I diagnosis, and does this differ by group? In exploratory analyses, we will ask whether any identified group differences in slopes deviate further when including lifetime axis-I diagnosis. To investigate putative interactions of FHR group and axis-I, we will start with the highest order, three-way interaction model. The rationale is that this will determine whether there are any group differences between subgroups (e.g., FHR-SZ with vs. without axis-I or FHR-SZ with axis-I vs. PBC without axis-I), which we will subsequently investigate with pairwise post hoc analyses. Regardless of the outcome, we will simplify the model, examining axis-I by age interactions for each group separately (i.e., stratified by group) to determine whether youths with axis-I diagnoses differ in their age-related cortical structural changes relative to those without an axis-I diagnosis, within each group. We predict that there will be an interaction with group such that the most pronounced effects will be observed in the FHR children with axis-I diagnoses. If we see significant group effects in step 1, the three-way interaction model would look like this:

lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age*axis-I + group*sex + age*sex + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))	

If we see significant group effects in step 2 for females, the three-way interaction model would look like this:

For females only: lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age*axis-I + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))

B.	Including psychotic-like experiences: Do developmental slopes differ based on psychotic-like experiences, and does this differ by group? We will incorporate an additional variable, psychotic-like experiences (PLEs), into new models based on those in the previous steps where there are group differences in slopes. Similar to axis-I, in exploratory analyses, we will ask whether the existing group differences in slopes deviate further when including PLE data from VIA 11 and VIA 15 (see Variables section for definition). 
We will again start with the highest order, three-way interaction model. The rationale is that this will determine whether there are any group differences between subgroups (e.g., FHR-SZ PLE+ vs. FHR-SZ PLE- or FHR-SZ PLE+ vs. PBC PLE-), which we will subsequently investigate with pairwise post hoc analyses. We predict that there will be an interaction with group such that the most pronounced structural changes will be observed in the FHR children with PLEs, and that these deviations will be strongest in those with PLEs already at VIA 11. Regardless of the outcome, as with axis-I, we will again simplify the model, examining PLE by age interactions for each group separately (i.e., stratified by group) to determine whether youths with PLEs deviate in their age-related cortical structural changes relative to those without PLEs, within each group. Lastly, we will simplify the models further and examine main effects of PLE across and within groups. We may also run the above models for a PLE variable reflecting PLEs in the last 6 months, as an additional exploratory analysis (the main PLE variable of interest reflects PLEs in the last 4 years; see Variables section). If we see significant group effects in step 1, the three-way interaction model would look like this:

lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age*PLE + group*sex + age*sex + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))

If we see significant group effects in step 2 for females, the three-way interaction model would look like this:

For females only: lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age*PLE + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))

C.	We will additionally rerun models controlling for intracranial volume (ICV) in order to compare analyses with and without ICV as an additional covariate, as doing this is recommended when studying developing children. Since skull growth and brain growth are highly correlated, we expect that ICV may explain most of the variance in the brain outcome measures and weaken any previously identified group effects.

We plan to run linear mixed-effects models including group, sex, age, group by sex, group by age, age by sex, site, and Euler number, with random intercepts for subject nested in families in order to account for sibling pairs. There are four structural brain measures of interest, as in the VIA 11 cortical paper, which are brain volume, cortical volume, surface area, and cortical thickness. As we have four brain measures of interest, we will use FDR correction for these four measures. Using the lme4 package in R, the models will look like this:

lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age + group*sex + age*sex + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))

We are primarily interested in interpreting the interaction terms for group by age and group by sex. We are including the group by sex interaction already in step 1 because we expect there to be sex-specific group differences given the findings from VIA 11. For group by age, we expect to see a reduction across time for each cortical structural brain measure in each group, which will be more pronounced in FHR-SZ. To ease interpretation, we will mean center age such that the main effect of group can be interpreted as the effect at the mean age, across the investigated age range. For group by sex, we expect to replicate results from VIA 11, namely to see reduced brain volume, cortical volume, and surface area in FHR-SZ males, and increased brain volume and cortical volume in FHR-BP females. We additionally expect to see reduced cortical thickness in FHR-SZ males, which was not previously seen in VIA 11 but is predicted now that data also extends to VIA 15, given the accelerated cortical thinning observed in adolescence. Age by sex is included as a control variable since we expect slopes to differ by sex (i.e., earlier maturation in females) although we are not primarily interested in this variability. We further control for MRI site and euler number.

Step 2: Testing group by age interactions, stratifying by sex
Whether or not the group by age or group by sex interactions are significant in step 1, we will proceed to step 2, since there is a strong justification to test for sex-specific group differences in slope between VIA 11 and VIA 15 given the sex-specific effects already identified in VIA 11. To test for sex-specific group differences, we will stratify the sample by sex and run linear mixed-effects models similar to those in step 1, including group, age, group by age, site, and Euler number, with random intercepts for subject nested in families. The models will look like this:

For females only: lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))

For males only: lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))

\tWe expect group effects similar to those observed in VIA 11. For group by age, similar to step 1, we expect to see a reduction across time for each cortical structural brain measure in each group, which will be more pronounced in FHR-SZ, for both females and males. Since accelerated cortical thinning starts earlier for females, we predict that reduced cortical thickness will extend to FHR-SZ females as well as males. One exception to the pattern of reduced cortical structural brain measures is FHR-BP females, who we predict will not show more pronounced significant age-related reductions in brain volume or cortical volume compared to PBC females at the whole group level. This is because they had larger brain volume and cortical volume in VIA 11, and studies of adult relatives of individuals with BP have larger volumes, so FHR-BP females may be on a different maturational trajectory.

Step 3: Testing group by age by sex interactions
Since sex differences cannot be formally tested in stratified models, we will test them in a three-way interaction (group by age by sex) in models that look like this:

lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age*sex + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))

In this model, we can directly test the effect of sex-specific group differences on slope between VIA 11 and VIA 15. As noted above, we predict that FHR-SZ females will have a steeper decline than FHR-SZ males, which will also be true though to a lesser extent for females in general. This is because FHR-SZ females do not show reductions in brain volume, cortical volume, surface area, or cortical thickness already in VIA 11, while FHR-SZ males do, and because we know that females in general show an earlier inflection point of cortical thinning during adolescence, or the age at which the rate of thinning is fastest. Conversely, we predict that FHR-BP females will decline less than FHR-BP males, particularly in brain volume and cortical volume, as these measures were increased in FHR-BP females in VIA 11. Generally, however, we do not expect major sex-specific group differences in slope.

Step 4: Planned follow-up analyses
Additionally, planned follow-up up analyses will be performed based on the findings from the previous steps. For example, if we see a significant group effect in step 1, then we would take the step 1 model and adjust it according to the planned follow-up analysis (e.g., adding an additional covariate). If we see a significant group effect in step 2, then we would also add to the model from step 2. We think that models from step 2 are the most likely to yield significant results and advance to the planned follow-up analyses.

A.\tIncluding lifetime axis-I diagnoses:

i.\tDo results survive when controlling for lifetime axis-I diagnoses? We will incorporate an additional covariate, lifetime axis-I diagnosis (excluding elimination disorders, unspecified tic disorder, and specific phobias), into new models based on those in the previous steps where there is a significant effect of group. We predict that including lifetime axis-I diagnoses will weaken the group effect, but that the group effect will remain significant. If we see significant group effects in step 1, the model controlling for axis-I would look like this:

lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age + group*sex + age*sex + axis-I + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))

If we see significant group effects in step 2 for females, the model controlling for axis-I would look like this:

For females only: lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age + axis-I + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))

ii.\tDo developmental slopes differ based on axis-I diagnosis, and does this differ by group? In exploratory analyses, we will ask whether any identified group differences in slopes deviate further when including lifetime axis-I diagnosis. To investigate putative interactions of FHR group and axis-I, we will start with the highest order, three-way interaction model. The rationale is that this will determine whether there are any group differences between subgroups (e.g., FHR-SZ with vs. without axis-I or FHR-SZ with axis-I vs. PBC without axis-I), which we will subsequently investigate with pairwise post hoc analyses. Regardless of the outcome, we will simplify the model, examining axis-I by age interactions for each group separately (i.e., stratified by group) to determine whether youths with axis-I diagnoses differ in their age-related cortical structural changes relative to those without an axis-I diagnosis, within each group. We predict that there will be an interaction with group such that the most pronounced effects will be observed in the FHR children with axis-I diagnoses. If we see significant group effects in step 1, the three-way interaction model would look like this:

lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age*axis-I + group*sex + age*sex + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))\t

If we see significant group effects in step 2 for females, the three-way interaction model would look like this:

For females only: lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age*axis-I + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))

B.\tIncluding psychotic-like experiences: Do developmental slopes differ based on psychotic-like experiences, and does this differ by group? We will incorporate an additional variable, psychotic-like experiences (PLEs), into new models based on those in the previous steps where there are group differences in slopes. Similar to axis-I, in exploratory analyses, we will ask whether the existing group differences in slopes deviate further when including PLE data from VIA 11 and VIA 15 (see Variables section for definition).
We will again start with the highest order, three-way interaction model. The rationale is that this will determine whether there are any group differences between subgroups (e.g., FHR-SZ PLE+ vs. FHR-SZ PLE- or FHR-SZ PLE+ vs. PBC PLE-), which we will subsequently investigate with pairwise post hoc analyses. We predict that there will be an interaction with group such that the most pronounced structural changes will be observed in the FHR children with PLEs, and that these deviations will be strongest in those with PLEs already at VIA 11. Regardless of the outcome, as with axis-I, we will again simplify the model, examining PLE by age interactions for each group separately (i.e., stratified by group) to determine whether youths with PLEs deviate in their age-related cortical structural changes relative to those without PLEs, within each group. Lastly, we will simplify the models further and examine main effects of PLE across and within groups. We may also run the above models for a PLE variable reflecting PLEs in the last 6 months, as an additional exploratory analysis (the main PLE variable of interest reflects PLEs in the last 4 years; see Variables section). If we see significant group effects in step 1, the three-way interaction model would look like this:

lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age*PLE + group*sex + age*sex + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))

If we see significant group effects in step 2 for females, the three-way interaction model would look like this:

For females only: lmer(brain_measure ~ group*age*PLE + site + euler_number + (1 | family_id / sub_id))

C.\tWe will additionally rerun models controlling for intracranial volume (ICV) in order to compare analyses with and without ICV as an additional covariate, as doing this is recommended when studying developing children. Since skull growth and brain growth are highly correlated, we expect that ICV may explain most of the variance in the brain outcome measures and weaken any previously identified group effects.
